{{Short description|Theorem in complex geometry}}
{{lowercase title}}

In [[complex geometry]], the '''<math>\partial \bar \partial</math> lemma''' (pronounced '''ddbar lemma''') is a [[mathematical lemma]] about the [[de Rham cohomology]] class of a [[complex differential form]]. The <math>\partial \bar \partial</math>-lemma is a result of [[Hodge theory]] and the [[Kähler identities]] on a [[Compact space|compact]] [[Kähler manifold]]. Sometimes it is also known as the <math>dd^c</math>-lemma, due to the use of a related operator <math display="inline">d^c = -\frac{i}{2}(\partial - \bar \partial)</math>, with the relation between the two operators being <math>i\partial \bar \partial = dd^c</math> and so <math>\alpha = dd^c \beta</math>.<ref name=":2" />{{Rp|location=1.17}}<ref name=":3" />{{Rp|location=Lem 5.50}}

==Statement==
The <math>\partial \bar \partial</math> lemma asserts that if <math>(X,\omega)</math> is a compact Kähler manifold and <math>\alpha \in \Omega^{p,q}(X)</math> is a complex differential form of bidegree (p,q) (with <math>p,q\ge 1</math>) whose class <math>[\alpha] \in H_{dR}^{p+q}(X,\mathbb{C})</math> is zero in de Rham cohomology, then there exists a form <math>\beta\in \Omega^{p-1,q-1}(X)</math> of bidegree (p-1,q-1) such that

<math display="block">\alpha = i\partial \bar \partial \beta,</math>

where <math>\partial</math> and <math>\bar \partial</math> are the [[Dolbeault operator]]s of the [[complex manifold]] <math>X</math>.<ref name=":0">{{cite book |isbn=9781571462343|title=Analytic Methods in Algebraic Geometry |last1=Demailly |first1=Jean-Pierre |year=2012|publisher= Somerville, MA: International Press.}}</ref>{{Rp|location=Ch VI Lem 8.6}}

===ddbar potential===
The form <math>\beta</math> is called the '''<math>\partial \bar \partial</math>-potential''' of <math>\alpha</math>. The inclusion of the factor <math>i</math> ensures that <math>i\partial \bar \partial</math> is a ''real'' differential operator, that is if <math>\alpha</math> is a differential form with real coefficients, then so is <math>\beta</math>.

This lemma should be compared to the notion of an [[exact differential form]] in de Rham cohomology. In particular if <math>\alpha\in \Omega^k(X)</math> is a [[closed and exact differential forms|closed]] differential k-form (on any smooth manifold) whose class is zero in de Rham cohomology, then <math>\alpha = d\gamma</math> for some differential (k-1)-form <math>\gamma</math> called the '''<math>d</math>-potential''' (or just '''potential''') of <math>\alpha</math>, where <math>d</math> is the [[exterior derivative]]. Indeed, since the Dolbeault operators sum to give the exterior derivative <math>d = \partial + \bar \partial</math> and <math>\bar \partial^2 = 0</math>, the <math>\partial \bar \partial</math>-lemma implies that we could have picked <math>\gamma = \bar \partial \beta </math>, refining the <math>d</math>-potential to the <math>\partial \bar \partial</math>-potential in the setting of compact Kähler manifolds.

== Proof ==
The <math>\partial \bar \partial</math>-lemma is a consequence of [[Hodge theory]] applied to a compact Kähler manifold.<ref name=":0" /><ref name=":2">{{cite book |last1=Gauduchon |first1=P. |title=Calabi's extremal Kähler metrics: An elementary introduction|chapter=Elements of Kähler geometry |date=2010|type=Preprint }}</ref>{{rp|41–44}}<ref name=":3">{{cite book |doi=10.4171/025|title=Lectures on Kähler Manifolds |year=2006 |last1=Ballmann |first1=Werner |isbn=978-3-03719-025-8|publisher=European mathematical society}}</ref>{{rp|73–77}}

The [[Hodge theory#Hodge theory of elliptic complexes|Hodge theorem for an elliptic complex]] may be applied to any of the operators <math>d, \partial, \bar \partial</math> and respectively to their [[Laplace operator|Laplace operators]] <math>\Delta_d, \Delta_{\partial}, \Delta_{\bar \partial}</math>. To these operators one can define spaces of harmonic differential forms given by the kernels:

<math display="block">\begin{align}
\mathcal{H}_d^k &= \ker \Delta_d : \Omega^k(X) \to \Omega^k(X)\\
\mathcal{H}_{\partial}^{p,q} &= \ker \Delta_{\partial}: \Omega^{p,q}(X) \to \Omega^{p,q}(X)\\
\mathcal{H}_{\bar \partial}^{p,q} &= \ker \Delta_{\bar \partial}: \Omega^{p,q}(X) \to \Omega^{p,q}(X)\\
\end{align} </math>

The Hodge decomposition theorem asserts that there are three orthogonal decompositions associated to these spaces of harmonic forms, given by

<math display="block">\begin{align}
\Omega^k(X) &= \mathcal{H}_d^k \oplus \operatorname{im} d \oplus \operatorname{im} d^*\\
\Omega^{p,q}(X) &= \mathcal{H}_{\partial}^{p,q} \oplus \operatorname{im} \partial \oplus \operatorname{im} \partial^*\\
\Omega^{p,q}(X) &= \mathcal{H}_{\bar \partial}^{p,q} \oplus \operatorname{im} \bar \partial \oplus \operatorname{im} \bar \partial^*
\end{align} </math>

where <math>d^*, \partial^*, \bar \partial^* </math> are the [[formal adjoint]]s of <math>d,\partial, \bar\partial </math> with respect to the [[Riemannian metric]] of the Kähler manifold, respectively.<ref name=":4">{{cite book |doi=10.1007/b137952|title=Complex Geometry |series=Universitext |year=2005 |isbn=3-540-21290-6|first=D.|last=Huybrechts|author-link=Daniel Huybrechts|publisher=Berlin: Springer}}</ref>{{Rp|location=Thm. 3.2.8}} These decompositions hold separately on any compact complex manifold. The importance of the manifold being Kähler is that there is a relationship between the Laplacians of <math>d,\partial,\bar \partial </math> and hence of the orthogonal decompositions above. In particular on a compact Kähler manifold

<math display="block">\Delta_d = 2 \Delta_{\partial} = 2 \Delta_{\bar \partial} </math>

which implies an orthogonal decomposition

<math display="block">\mathcal{H}_d^k = \bigoplus_{p+q=k} \mathcal{H}_{\partial}^{p,q} = \bigoplus_{p+q=k} \mathcal{H}_{\bar \partial}^{p,q} </math>

where there are the further relations <math>\mathcal{H}_{\partial}^{p,q} = \overline{\mathcal{H}_{\bar \partial}^{q,p}}</math> relating the spaces of <math>\partial </math> and <math>\bar \partial </math>-harmonic forms.<ref name=":4" />{{Rp|location=Prop. 3.1.12}}

As a result of the above decompositions, one can prove the following lemma.

{{math theorem
| math_statement = Let <math>\alpha\in \Omega^{p,q}(X)</math> be a <math>d</math>-closed (p,q)-form on a compact Kähler manifold <math>X</math>. Then the following are equivalent:
{{Ordered list|list_style_type=lower-alpha|<math>\alpha</math> is <math>d</math>-exact.|<math>\alpha</math> is <math>\partial</math>-exact.|<math>\alpha</math> is <math>\bar \partial</math>-exact.|<math>\alpha</math> is <math>\partial \bar \partial</math>-exact. That is there exists <math>\beta</math> such that <math>\alpha = i \partial \bar \partial \beta</math>.|<math>\alpha</math> is orthogonal to <math>\mathcal{H}_{\bar \partial}^{p,q}\subset \Omega^{p,q}(X)</math>.}}
| name = Lemma (<math>\partial \bar \partial</math>-lemma)<ref name=":0" />{{rp|311}}
}}

The proof is as follows.<ref name=":4" />{{Rp|location=Cor. 3.2.10}} Let <math>\alpha\in \Omega^{p,q}(X) </math> be a closed (p,q)-form on a compact Kähler manifold <math>(X,\omega)</math>. It follows quickly that (d) implies (a), (b), and (c). Moreover, the orthogonal decompositions above imply that any of (a), (b), or (c) imply (e). Therefore, the main difficulty is to show that (e) implies (d).

To that end, suppose that <math>\alpha</math> is orthogonal to the subspace <math>\mathcal{H}_{\bar \partial}^{p,q} \subset \Omega^{p,q}(X)</math>. Then <math>\alpha \in \operatorname{im} \bar \partial \oplus \operatorname{im} \bar \partial^*</math>. Since <math>\alpha</math> is <math>d</math>-closed and <math>d=\partial + \bar \partial</math>, it is also <math>\bar \partial</math>-closed (that is <math>\bar \partial \alpha = 0</math>). If <math>\alpha = \alpha' + \alpha''</math> where <math>\alpha' \in \operatorname{im} \bar \partial</math> and <math>\alpha'' = \bar \partial^* \gamma</math> is contained in <math>\operatorname{im} \bar \partial^*</math> then since this sum is from an orthogonal decomposition with respect to the inner product <math>\langle - , - \rangle</math> induced by the Riemannian metric,

<math display="block">\langle \alpha'', \alpha''\rangle = \langle \alpha, \alpha'' \rangle = \langle \alpha, \bar \partial^* \gamma \rangle = \langle \bar \partial \alpha, \gamma \rangle = 0</math>

or in other words <math>\|\alpha''\|^2 = 0</math> and <math>\alpha'' = 0</math>. Thus it is the case that <math>\alpha=\alpha'\in \operatorname{im} \bar \partial</math>. This allows us to write <math>\alpha = \bar \partial \eta</math> for some differential form <math>\eta \in \Omega^{p,q-1}(X)</math>. Applying the Hodge decomposition for <math>\partial</math> to <math>\eta</math>,

<math display="block">\eta = \eta_0 + \partial \eta' + \partial^* \eta''</math>

where <math>\eta_0</math> is <math>\Delta_\partial</math>-harmonic, <math>\eta'\in \Omega^{p-1,q-1}(X)</math> and <math>\eta'' \in \Omega^{p+1,q-1}(X)</math>. The equality <math>\Delta_\bar \partial = \Delta_\partial</math> implies that <math>\eta_0</math> is also <math>\Delta_{\bar \partial}</math>-harmonic and therefore <math>\bar \partial \eta_0 = \bar \partial^* \eta_0 = 0</math>. Thus <math>\alpha = \bar \partial \partial \eta' + \bar \partial \partial^* \eta''</math>. However, since <math>\alpha</math> is <math>d</math>-closed, it is also <math>\partial</math>-closed. Then using a similar trick to above,

<math display="block">\langle \bar \partial \partial^* \eta'', \bar \partial \partial^* \eta''\rangle = \langle \alpha, \bar \partial \partial^* \eta'' \rangle = - \langle \alpha, \partial^* \bar \partial \eta'' \rangle = - \langle \partial \alpha, \bar \partial \eta'' \rangle = 0,</math>

also applying the [[Kähler identities|Kähler identity]] that <math>\bar \partial \partial^* = -\partial^* \bar \partial </math>. Thus <math>\alpha = \bar \partial \partial \eta'</math> and setting <math>\beta = i \eta' </math> produces the <math>\partial \bar \partial</math>-potential.

== Local version ==
A local version of the <math>\partial \bar \partial</math>-lemma holds and can be proven without the need to appeal to the Hodge decomposition theorem.<ref name=":4" />{{Rp|location=Ex 1.3.3, Rmk 3.2.11}} It is the analogue of the [[Poincaré lemma]] or [[Dolbeault cohomology#Dolbeault–Grothendieck lemma|Dolbeault–Grothendieck lemma]] for the <math>\partial \bar \partial</math> operator. The local <math>\partial \bar \partial</math>-lemma holds over any domain on which the aforementioned lemmas hold.

{{math theorem
| math_statement = Let <math>X</math> be a complex manifold and <math>\alpha\in \Omega^{p,q}(X)</math> be a differential form of bidegree (p,q) for <math>p,q\ge 1</math>. Then <math>\alpha</math> is <math>d</math>-closed if and only if for every point <math>p\in X</math> there exists an open neighbourhood <math>U\subset X</math> containing <math>p</math> and a differential form <math>\beta\in \Omega^{p-1,q-1}(U)</math> such that <math>\alpha = i \partial \bar \partial \beta</math> on <math>U</math>.
| name = Lemma (Local <math>\partial \bar \partial</math>-lemma)
}}

The proof follows quickly from the aforementioned lemmas. Firstly observe that if <math>\alpha</math> is locally of the form <math>\alpha = i\partial \bar \partial \beta</math> for some <math>\beta</math> then <math>d\alpha = d(i\partial \bar \partial \beta) = i (\partial + \bar \partial)(\partial \bar \partial \beta) = 0</math> because <math>\partial^2 = 0</math>, <math>\bar \partial^2=0</math>, and <math>\partial \bar \partial = - \bar \partial \partial</math>. On the other hand, suppose <math>\alpha</math> is <math>d</math>-closed. Then by the Poincaré lemma there exists an open neighbourhood <math>U</math> of any point <math>p\in X</math> and a form <math>\gamma\in \Omega^{p+q-1}(U)</math> such that <math>\alpha = d \gamma</math>. Now writing <math>\gamma = \gamma' + \gamma''</math> for <math>\gamma'\in \Omega^{p-1,q}(X)</math> and <math>\gamma'' \in \Omega^{p,q-1}(X)</math> note that <math>d\alpha = (\partial + \bar \partial) \alpha = 0</math> and comparing the bidegrees of the forms in <math>d\alpha</math> implies that <math>\bar \partial \gamma' = 0</math> and <math>\partial \gamma'' = 0</math> and that <math>\alpha = \partial \gamma' + \bar \partial \gamma''</math>. After possibly shrinking the size of the open neighbourhood <math>U</math>, the Dolbeault–Grothendieck lemma may be applied to <math>\gamma'</math> and <math>\overline{\gamma''}</math> (the latter because <math>\overline{ \partial \gamma''} = \bar \partial (\overline{\gamma''}) = 0</math>) to obtain local forms <math>\eta', \eta''\in \Omega^{p-1,q-1}(X)</math> such that <math>\gamma' = \bar \partial \eta'</math> and <math>\overline{\gamma''} = \bar \partial \eta''</math>. Noting then that <math>\gamma'' = \partial \overline{\eta''}</math> this completes the proof as <math>\alpha = \partial \bar \partial \eta' + \bar \partial \partial \overline{\eta''} = i\partial \bar \partial \beta</math> where <math>\beta = -i \eta' + i \overline{\eta''}</math>.

== Bott–Chern cohomology ==
The Bott–Chern cohomology is a cohomology theory for compact complex manifolds which depends on the operators <math>\partial</math> and <math>\bar \partial</math>, and measures the extent to which the <math>\partial \bar \partial</math>-lemma fails to hold. In particular when a compact complex manifold is a Kähler manifold, the Bott–Chern cohomology is isomorphic to the [[Dolbeault cohomology]], but in general it contains more information.

The '''Bott–Chern cohomology groups''' of a compact complex manifold<ref name=":0" /> are defined by

<math display="block">H_{BC}^{p,q}(X) = \frac{ \ker (\partial: \Omega^{p,q} \to \Omega^{p+1,q}) \cap \ker (\bar \partial: \Omega^{p,q} \to \Omega^{p,q+1})}{\operatorname{im} (\partial \bar \partial: \Omega^{p-1,q-1} \to \Omega^{p,q})}.</math>

Since a differential form which is both <math>\partial</math> and <math>\bar \partial</math>-closed is <math>d</math>-closed, there is a natural map <math>H_{BC}^{p,q}(X) \to H_{dR}^{p+q}(X,\mathbb{C})</math> from Bott–Chern cohomology groups to de Rham cohomology groups. There are also maps to the <math>\partial</math> and <math>\bar \partial</math> Dolbeault cohomology groups <math>H_{BC}^{p,q}(X) \to H_{\partial}^{p,q}(X), H_{\bar \partial}^{p,q}(X)</math>. When the manifold <math>X</math> satisfies the <math>\partial \bar \partial</math>-lemma, for example if it is a compact Kähler manifold, then the above maps from Bott–Chern cohomology to Dolbeault cohomology are isomorphisms, and furthermore the map from Bott–Chern cohomology to de Rham cohomology is injective.<ref name=":1">{{cite journal |doi=10.1007/s00222-012-0406-3|title=On the <math>\partial \bar \partial</math>-Lemma and Bott-Chern cohomology |year=2013 |last1=Angella |first1=Daniele |last2=Tomassini |first2=Adriano |journal=Inventiones Mathematicae |volume=192 |pages=71–81 |s2cid=253747048 |arxiv=1402.1954 }}</ref> As a consequence, there is an isomorphism

<math display="block">H_{dR}^{k}(X,\mathbb{C}) = \bigoplus_{p+q=k} H_{BC}^{p,q}(X)</math>

whenever <math>X</math> satisfies the <math>\partial \bar \partial</math>-lemma. In this way, the kernel of the maps above measure the failure of the manifold <math>X</math> to satisfy the lemma, and in particular measure the failure of <math>X</math> to be a Kähler manifold.

==Consequences for bidegree (1,1)==
The most significant consequence of the <math>\partial \bar \partial</math>-lemma occurs when the complex differential form has bidegree (1,1). In this case the lemma states that an [[exact differential form]] <math>\alpha\in \Omega^{1,1}(X)</math> has a <math>\partial \bar \partial</math>-potential given by a [[Smoothness|smooth function]] <math>f\in C^{\infty}(X,\mathbb{C})</math>:

<math display="block">\alpha = i\partial \bar \partial f.</math>

In particular this occurs in the case where <math>\alpha = \omega</math> is a Kähler form restricted to a small [[Open set|open subset]] <math>U \subset X</math> of a Kähler manifold (this case follows from the [[Ddbar lemma#Local version|local version]] of the lemma), where the aforementioned Poincaré lemma ensures that it is an exact differential form. This leads to the notion of a [[Kahler potential|Kähler potential]], a locally defined function which completely specifies the Kähler form. Another important case is when <math>\alpha = \omega - \omega'</math> is the difference of two Kähler forms which are in the same de Rham cohomology class <math>[\omega] = [\omega']</math>. In this case <math>[\alpha] = [\omega] - [\omega'] = 0</math> in de Rham cohomology so the <math>\partial \bar \partial</math>-lemma applies. By allowing (differences of) Kähler forms to be completely described using a single function, which is automatically a [[plurisubharmonic function]], the study of compact Kähler manifolds can be undertaken using techniques of [[pluripotential theory]], for which many [[Mathematical analysis|analytical]] tools are available. For example, the <math>\partial \bar \partial</math>-lemma is used to rephrase the [[Kähler–Einstein metric|Kähler–Einstein equation]] in terms of potentials, transforming it into a complex [[Monge–Ampère equation]] for the Kähler potential.

==ddbar manifolds==
Complex manifolds which are not necessarily Kähler but still happen to satisfy the <math>\partial \bar \partial</math>-lemma are known as <math>\partial \bar \partial</math>-manifolds. For example, compact complex manifolds which are [[Fujiki class C]] satisfy the <math>\partial \bar \partial</math>-lemma but are not necessarily Kähler.<ref name=":1" />
